transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. How can I help you today?

Well, I... I suppose I'm here because things have just gotten so out of hand lately. It's my face, specifically the lower half of my face. I just... I can't stop seeing this awful droop, this terrible unevenness around my mouth and my jawline. It's like, every time I catch a glimpse of myself in a mirror, or a window, or God forbid, a photograph... it's just glaring at me. It's all I can see. And I know people say, "Oh, you look fine, it's just aging, you look great for fifty-four," but they're just being polite, they have to be. Because to me, it feels so obvious, so hideous, that it's actually starting to ruin my work. I'm an architect, you know, and I have to pitch designs, I have to stand up in front of clients and boards, and lately... I just can't do it. I've been avoiding presentations entirely. I make up excuses to not meet clients in person because I just know they're staring at my jaw, wondering what's wrong with my face. It's just exhausting, constantly trying to hide it, constantly thinking about it. I mean, it's taking over my life, it really is.
How much time do you typically spend each day thinking about the appearance of your jawline or mouth?

Oh, how much time? I... I don't even know how to quantify it, really, because it feels like it's just always there. It's not like I sit down and say, "Okay, from two to three o'clock, I'm going to worry about my jaw." It's... it's a constant, low-level hum in the background of my mind, and then it flares up into these huge, overwhelming episodes. 

Like, I'll wake up, right? And before I even get out of bed, I'm already dreading the bathroom mirror. I'll lie there for maybe twenty, thirty minutes, just running my fingers along my jawline, feeling for the slackness, trying to pull the skin back towards my ears to see what it would look like if it were just... normal. And then I have to get up, and the whole time I'm brushing my teeth, I'm staring. I'll lean in so close to the glass, turning my head this way and that, checking the lighting. If it's overcast outside, the shadows hit my face differently, and it makes the drooping look ten times worse. So I'll spend, I don't know, maybe an hour just trying different angles, trying to find a way to hold my neck so it's less noticeable. 

And then at work... oh, at work it's impossible. I have this beautiful, open-plan office—I designed it myself, actually, lots of natural light, glass partitions—and it used to be my pride and joy. But now, every reflective surface is a trap. I'll be drafting, and I'll catch my reflection in my monitor, and that's it. My concentration is gone. I'll spend the next forty-five minutes just fixating on it, taking pictures with my phone to see if it looks as bad as I think it does, and then deleting them immediately because I can't bear to look at them. I'll go to the restroom just to check the mirror again, maybe five or six times a day, easily spending fifteen minutes each time just... agonizing over it. 

Even when I'm driving home, I'm adjusting the rearview mirror so I can check my profile at stoplights. And in the evening, instead of relaxing, I'm researching procedures, or looking at old photos from ten years ago, comparing them to now, just crying over how much my face has collapsed. So if you ask me how much time... I mean, it has to be hours. Four, five, maybe six hours a day of active, intense scrutiny, but really, it's occupying my thoughts from the moment I wake up until the moment I finally manage to fall asleep. It's just exhausting.
Have you been feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?

Oh, feeling down... yes. Yes, I suppose I have been. But it's... it's all so tied up with this, you know? It's hard to separate it. Like, you asked about losing interest in things. I used to love going to art galleries. I mean, as an architect, visual arts are so important to me, so inspiring. My husband and I used to go to openings all the time downtown, have a glass of wine, mingle... I haven't been to one in months. Not in months. 

And it's not that I don't care about the art anymore, it's just... the thought of being in those bright, unforgiving gallery lights, surrounded by all those put-together people... I just can't stomach it. I picture myself standing there, trying to discuss a painting, and all I can think is that whoever I'm talking to is just staring at my sagging jaw. So I just stay home. I tell my husband I'm tired, or I have a headache, or I need to catch up on work—which is a joke, really, because I can barely focus on work anyway. 

And as for feeling hopeless... well, how could I not? I look in the mirror and I just see this... this deterioration that I can't stop. I've tried all these expensive creams, these facial exercises I found online, I even bought one of those ridiculous microcurrent devices, and nothing works. It just keeps getting worse. I sit on the couch at night, and I just feel this heavy, sinking feeling in my chest, like my best years are completely behind me and I'm just going to fade into this ugly, irrelevant background character. I used to be so vibrant, you know? I used to command a room. And now I just want to hide in the dark. It's just so bleak. It really is. I just feel like crying all the time, honestly.

Do you find yourself repeating certain behaviors or mental acts—like checking mirrors, adjusting your face, or going over your appearance in your mind—in response to your concerns about your jawline or mouth?

Oh, absolutely. I know I mentioned the mirrors earlier, but it's... it's a whole ordeal. It's not just a quick glance, it's a complete compulsion. Especially before work, or, heaven forbid, a family event. We had my niece's engagement party recently, and I... well, I can spend hours, literally hours, just trapped in the bathroom. 

I'll start by checking the bathroom mirror, leaning in so close my breath fogs the glass. And then I pull out my phone. I must take dozens of pictures of myself from every conceivable angle—straight on, profile, chin up, chin down—just trying to see exactly how bad the drooping is, how obvious it is to everyone else. And then the panic sets in, so I try to fix it. I'll do my makeup, try to use contouring to create some illusion of a jawline, but then it looks too heavy, so I wash it all off and start completely over. I've redone my makeup three or four times in a single morning. 

And then come the scarves. I've bought an entire wardrobe of silk scarves lately, just for this. I'll tie one around my neck, trying to drape it so it camouflages the slack skin, but then I think it looks too suspicious, like I'm obviously hiding something. So I untie it, try a different knot, try a different scarf... just over and over. 

And my poor husband, I drive him absolutely out of his mind. I'll walk out to the kitchen and ask him, "Does my face look lopsided today? Is the left side hanging lower than the right?" And I make him really look at me. And he always sighs and says I look fine, but I know he's just exhausted by it, which makes me feel even worse. 

But I still can't let it go. Even after we get in the car, or when I finally sit down at my desk, I'll be on my phone, scrolling through social media or professional directories, just obsessively looking at photos of other women my age. I'll find women in their fifties and I just stare at their jawlines, zooming in, comparing their tight skin to my sagging face, just torturing myself to see how bad mine looks beside theirs. It's like I have to prove to myself how hideous I am. It's just this endless, exhausting loop, and I can't seem to stop myself from doing it, day after day.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms align most closely with F45.22 (Body Dysmorphic Disorder), given the persistent preoccupation with a perceived defect in appearance (jawline asymmetry), repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, scarves, makeup rituals), and significant impairment in functioning. Depression and anxiety features are present but appear secondary to the core body image concerns, which rules out F32.3 (Major Depressive Disorder, Severe) and F40.00 (Social Phobia).
